script.opening: "I’ve had this sore on the inside of my ankle for a few weeks now — it weeps and it just won’t heal. My neighbour had hers bandaged up tight and it sorted it, so can you just do that for me? My leg’s swollen and a bit itchy round it too."

facts.text: Right leg, just above the inner ankle bone. Started about 7 weeks ago after she knocked it on the shopping trolley. "It just broke down." Weeps a lot — soaks through dressings. Not bleeding. Can show it to the camera if asked; the nurse dressed it this morning and took a photo.
"Not really painful — sore when the dressing sticks." No pain in the calf or foot when walking, no pain at night in bed, doesn’t hang her leg out of the bed to ease it. Feet not cold.

Ankles swell by evening, better in the morning. Skin round the ankle has gone brown over the years, and itchy and flaky. Varicose veins "since my second baby". No calf swelling that came on suddenly, no breathlessness.

Overweight; walks with a stick, mostly sits in her chair. No diabetes she knows of. Blood pressure tablets (amlodipine). No heart attack, stroke or circulation problems known. Never smoked. No allergies (had a rash from a sticky plaster once).
No fever, no spreading redness, no bad smell, feels well.
Widow, lives alone in a ground-floor flat. Daughter visits weekly. Can get to the surgery by taxi. Finds the weeping embarrassing — "it smells sometimes and soaks through my stockings".

Chatty, pleasant, a bit stubborn. You keep coming back to "the tight bandage like my neighbour’s". If told it can’t be done until the circulation test, be disappointed ("So you can’t do it today?") but accept if the reason is explained and something is started now. Ask whether you need antibiotics.

ice.ideas: "A tight bandage sorted my neighbour’s, so it’ll sort mine."
ice.concerns: "That it’ll never heal. And it’s so wet, it’s embarrassing — I don’t want people smelling it." Secret worry: her late husband had a leg amputated (diabetes) and she fears the same.
ice.expectations: "For you to bandage it up tight, today."

checkpoints.text: Assesses the chronic leg ulcer and distinguishes VENOUS (gaiter area, shallow/exudative, haemosiderin/varicose eczema/oedema, pulses present) from ARTERIAL (distal/punched-out, deep, painful, cold/pale foot, absent pulses) and neuropathic causes — using the nurse’s recorded findings and photo (site, edges, exudate, skin changes, oedema, pulses, capillary refill) and arranging ABPI

Recognises that COMPRESSION is the mainstay of venous-ulcer healing but that the ANKLE-BRACHIAL PRESSURE INDEX (ABPI) must be measured before STRONG compression to exclude significant arterial disease (mild compression of 20 mmHg or less can start now if there are no red flags, with ABPI normally within 14 days — NWCSP) — because compression on an arterial leg risks ischaemia/necrosis (so "bandage it tight" is unsafe until confirmed)

Keeps the must-not-miss in mind — a non-healing or atypical ulcer (rolled/everted edges) may be a skin malignancy (SCC/Marjolin’s) warranting biopsy/specialist assessment (NICE NG12: consider a suspected cancer pathway referral if SCC is suspected) — and reconsiders the diagnosis if healing fails

Manages the venous ulcer once ABPI is adequate — referral to leg-ulcer/tissue-viability/district nursing for graded compression, wound care, elevation/oedema management, varicose-eczema treatment, venous-disease assessment (vascular referral for an ulcer not healed within 2 weeks, NICE CG168) — with antibiotics only if clinically infected
Gives lifestyle/prevention advice (weight, mobility/calf activity, elevation, skin care) and post-healing compression hosiery to prevent recurrence, with ongoing nursing follow-up
Takes the "bandage it tight" request seriously and explains WHY ABPI must come before strong compression (safety) without dismissing her, setting realistic expectations about slow venous healing
Checks understanding and engages her in the plan (assessment, leg-ulcer service, follow-up) rather than simply applying compression on request

Safety-nets and follows up: ABPI and leg-ulcer-service referral, signs of infection/arterial compromise (increasing pain, cold/pale/dusky foot) warranting urgent review, malignancy awareness for non-healing, and review — ABPI before strong compression, not bandaging on request

worked.txt: "I can see why — a tight bandage often is the treatment for this kind of ulcer, and your neighbour’s right that it works. But there’s an important safety check first, because for some people tight bandaging can actually be harmful. Let me explain."

"This sore is over your inner ankle with the brown staining and swelling around it — that fits a venous ulcer, from the leg veins not draining well. The nurse’s note and photo this morning help a lot — she could feel the pulses in your foot, which is reassuring, and we’ll check the circulation properly with a simple ankle test."

"Before any tight, strong compression, I need to check the blood supply to your foot with a simple test called the ABPI — ankle and arm blood pressures. If the arteries are narrowed, tight bandaging could cut off the circulation, which is dangerous. So we confirm it’s safe first — that’s why I can’t just bandage it tightly today. If nothing worrying turns up, the nurses can start a light support bandage straight away while we arrange that test."

"Assuming the blood supply is fine, I’ll refer you to the leg-ulcer nursing service, and to the vein specialists to look at the veins underneath, for proper graded compression and dressings, plus elevating the leg and looking after the skin. Venous ulcers do heal, but I’ll be honest — it can take weeks to months, so we’ll be patient."
"If an ulcer doesn’t heal as expected or looks unusual, we’d take a small sample to be sure of the cause — just being thorough. I’ll keep an eye on it."

"Longer term — keeping moving, losing a little weight, elevating the leg and wearing support stockings once healed all help prevent it coming back. Come back urgently if the foot becomes cold, pale, very painful or the area looks infected. We’ll get the assessment booked."

f.learning: Assess a chronic LEG ULCER by distinguishing VENOUS ulcers (over the medial GAITER area, shallow with sloping edges, exudative, surrounded by haemosiderin staining, varicose eczema and oedema, relatively less painful, with palpable foot pulses) from ARTERIAL ulcers (distal sites/pressure points, "punched-out", deep, painful especially at night and on elevation, cold/pale foot, absent/weak pulses) and neuropathic ulcers (pressure points in diabetics), using recorded findings from the nurse (photograph, pulses, capillary refill, sensation) when consulting remotely and arranging ABPI. The safety-critical, examinable point is that although COMPRESSION is the mainstay of venous-ulcer healing, the ANKLE-BRACHIAL PRESSURE INDEX (ABPI) must be measured before STRONG compression to exclude significant arterial disease (NWCSP: mild compression of 20 mmHg or less can start straight away if there are no red flags, with ABPI normally within 14 days) — applying compression to a leg with arterial insufficiency can cause ischaemia, necrosis and limb loss — so "just bandage it up tight" is unsafe until arterial supply is confirmed adequate (broadly ABPI ~0.8–1.3 acceptable; outside that → vascular referral, no/modified compression). Keep the must-not-miss in mind: a non-healing or atypical ulcer (rolled/everted edges, exuberant granulation, bleeding) may be a skin malignancy (SCC, including Marjolin’s ulcer in chronic wounds/scars) warranting biopsy/specialist assessment, and reconsider the diagnosis if a "venous" ulcer fails to heal. Once ABPI confirms adequate supply, manage the venous ulcer via the leg-ulcer/tissue-viability/district-nursing service (graded compression, wound care/dressings, elevation and oedema management, varicose-eczema treatment, venous-disease assessment, with vascular referral for an ulcer not healed within 2 weeks per NICE CG168), treating infection with antibiotics only if clinically infected (NICE NG152). Advise on lifestyle/prevention (weight, mobility, elevation, skin care, post-healing compression hosiery as venous ulcers recur). The hidden agenda is the wish to be "bandaged tight"; explain why ABPI must come first, set realistic expectations of slow healing, and safety-net for infection/arterial compromise. A typical venous ulcer does not need a NICE NG12 suspected cancer pathway referral, but a non-healing/atypical ulcer prompts biopsy, and NG12 advises considering a suspected cancer pathway referral for a skin lesion that raises the suspicion of SCC.

knowledge.guideline: [1] National Wound Care Strategy Programme (NWCSP) Leg ulcer recommendations (2020, updated 2023) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · [2] NICE CG168 Varicose veins: diagnosis and management (2013) · [3] NICE NG152 Leg ulcer infection: antimicrobial prescribing (2020) · [5] NICE CG147 Peripheral arterial disease (2012, updated 2020)
knowledge.summary: A classic venous leg ulcer in the gaiter area. Compression heals it, but strong compression must wait for an ABPI to exclude arterial disease. Mild compression can start now if there are no red flags. Refer to the vascular service, treat infection only if present, and keep malignancy in mind if it does not heal.

points.t: Venous: medial gaiter area, shallow, sloping edges, exudate, haemosiderin staining, varicose eczema, oedema, often less painful. Arterial: distal or over pressure points, punched out, deep, painful especially at night or on elevation and eased by hanging the leg down, cold pale foot, weak or absent pulses. Neuropathic: pressure points in people with diabetes, often painless.

NWCSP [1]: if there are no red flags and no signs of arterial disease, start mild graduated compression (20 mmHg or less at the ankle) straight away, and complete a full assessment including ABPI, normally within 14 days. Strong, full compression, which is what “bandaged tight” means, is applied only after the ABPI. If the ABPI is below 0.8 or above 1.3, get specialist advice before compression.

Strong compression on a leg with poor arterial supply can cause ischaemia, necrosis and limb loss. Pulses alone are unreliable, especially with oedema and obesity. In diabetes, ABPI can be falsely normal or raised because the arteries are stiff [5].

CG168 [2]: refer people with a venous leg ulcer (a break in the skin below the knee that has not healed within 2 weeks) or a healed venous leg ulcer to a vascular service for duplex assessment and treatment of the underlying veins.

NG152 [3]: most leg ulcers are colonised and few are infected. Offer an antibiotic only if there are symptoms or signs of infection, such as redness or swelling spreading beyond the ulcer, local warmth, increased pain or fever. Do not swab routinely.

Rolled or everted edges, overgrown tissue, bleeding, an unusual site, or failure to heal despite good treatment should prompt reassessment and biopsy. NICE NG12 [4]: consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for a skin lesion that raises the suspicion of squamous cell carcinoma.

model.text: Hello Mrs Hart, I’m Dr Evans. What can I do for you today?

I’ve had this sore on the inside of my ankle for a few weeks now. It weeps and it just won’t heal. My neighbour had hers bandaged up tight and it sorted it, so can you just do that for me? My leg’s swollen and a bit itchy round it too.

It sounds like it’s been a real nuisance for weeks. Your neighbour may well be right that a bandage is the answer, and I want to make sure it’s the right one for your leg. Can I ask a few questions and have a look on the camera?
model.why: Takes the request seriously; signals a plan

model.text: Go on then.
How did it start, and has it changed at all: bigger, bleeding, or looking different at the edges?
model.why: History of the ulcer, including atypical features

model.text: It just broke down. It’s about the same, just wet all the time. No bleeding.
Is it painful? Does your foot or calf hurt at night in bed, or when you put the leg up, and feel better hanging the leg over the side?
Not really painful. Sore when the dressing sticks. No, not at night.
Any pain in your calves when you walk that makes you stop? And do you have diabetes, or has anyone mentioned your circulation before?
model.why: Claudication, diabetes and known arterial disease

model.text: I don’t walk far. I don’t have diabetes that I know of.
Has the area become hot, redder, or more painful, or have you felt feverish?
No. Just itchy around it.
Can you show me both legs on the camera, close up on the sore? I can also see the nurse’s check of your foot pulses and the feeling in your feet in your notes.
model.why: Inspects both legs on video and uses the recorded pulses and sensation

model.text: The sore is shallow, just above the inside ankle bone, with brown staining and dry, itchy skin around it, and your ankle is swollen. That fits a venous ulcer, where the leg veins don’t drain properly. The edges look flat, which is reassuring. The nurse could feel the pulses, but swelling makes them hard to judge.
model.why: Describes venous features; notes the limits of the recorded pulse check

model.text: So I can have the bandage?
We’re getting there. Before I explain, what worries you most about it?
That it’ll never heal. And it’s so wet, it’s embarrassing.
That makes sense. With the right treatment most of these do heal, although it takes time.

Firm bandaging is the main treatment for this kind of ulcer. But a tight bandage squeezes the leg, and if the arteries bringing blood to the foot are narrowed, it can cut off the blood supply and do real harm. So first we measure the blood pressure at your ankles and arms and compare them. It’s called an ABPI.
model.why: Explains why ABPI must precede strong compression

model.text: So you can’t do it today?

The nurse can put on a light support bandage from today, which is safe because you don’t have signs of circulation problems. The proper tight bandaging starts once the test confirms the blood supply is good. I’ll book the test in the next week or two.
model.why: Mild compression now, full compression after ABPI (NWCSP)

model.text: That’s better than nothing.

I’d also like to refer you to the vascular team to look at your veins with a scan, as treating them can help the ulcer heal and stop it coming back. The nurses will do the dressings, and I’ll suggest a moisturiser for the itchy skin.
model.why: Vascular referral (CG168), wound care, varicose eczema

model.text: I don’t need antibiotics?
Not at the moment. Almost all ulcers have germs on the surface, but antibiotics only help if it becomes infected: spreading redness, heat, more pain or fever.
Raising your leg when you sit, and gentle ankle movements help the swelling. If you ever want support with weight, we can help with that too. How does that sound?
model.why: Lifestyle advice offered, not imposed; checks agreement

model.text: I can put my feet up more.

If the foot goes cold, pale or blue, or becomes very painful under the bandage, take the bandage off and contact us the same day. The same applies if the area goes red and hot or you feel feverish. If it’s not getting smaller after a few weeks, or the edges change or it bleeds, we’ll take a small sample to check the cause. Can you tell me what the plan is?
model.why: Compression and infection safety-net; malignancy awareness; teach-back

model.text: Light bandage now, the ankle test soon, then the tight one. Legs up. Take it off and ring if my foot goes cold or it hurts badly.
Perfect. I’ll see you after the test to go through the result.

social.t: Reduced mobility and weight make elevation, calf exercise and dressing changes harder. Ask what help she has at home and whether she can reach the leg-ulcer clinic or needs district nurses.
Leaking exudate is embarrassing and isolating. Good dressings and compression reduce it.

legal.t: Explain the benefits and risks of compression, including what to do if the foot becomes cold or painful, and record her consent.

professional.t: Practice nurses, district nurses, the tissue viability team and the vascular service share care. A clear referral and a documented ABPI keep the plan safe.
Apply NICE NG152: treat infection, not colonisation, and avoid routine swabs.

community.t: Community leg-ulcer clinics or leg clubs, where available, offer treatment and social contact. Legs Matter provides patient information.

redFlags: Rest pain at night or on elevation, cold or pale foot: arterial disease
Spreading redness, warmth, increasing pain or fever: infection
Rolled or everted edges, bleeding, overgrowth or failure to heal: possible SCC
Diabetes: neuropathic ulcer and unreliable ABPI
ice: Idea: a tight bandage will cure it, as it did for her neighbour
Concern: that it will never heal

playbook.diagnosis: “This is a venous leg ulcer. The veins in your leg aren’t pushing blood back up efficiently, so the pressure in the skin near the ankle is high and it breaks down.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Imagine the veins as a pipe with one-way valves. When the valves are leaky, fluid pools at the ankle like water at the bottom of a hose. The bandage squeezes it back up. But we must check the supply pipe, the arteries, is open before we squeeze hard.”

management.reflectIce: “You’re right that a firm bandage is the treatment. We’re doing it safely: a light one now, and the full one once the test shows your circulation can take it.”
management.psychosocial: Arrange nursing care she can reach, support elevation and mobility, and offer weight support if she wants it.
sharedPlan: Mild compression now (no red flags), ABPI within 14 days (NWCSP)
Strong compression if ABPI 0.8–1.3; specialist advice otherwise
Dressings, emollient for varicose eczema, elevation
Antibiotics only if infected (NG152); consider HbA1c
safetyNet: Remove bandage and call same day for a cold, pale, blue or very painful foot
Call for spreading redness, heat or fever
Biopsy if not healing or atypical; review after ABPI

pitfalls.intro: This station hinges on one safety step. Candidates fail by bandaging on request or by refusing without explaining. The marks go to a safe compression plan, clear reasons, and stewardship.

items.fail: Applying strong compression without an ABPI.
items.why: Compression on a leg with arterial disease can cause necrosis.
items.fix: Mild compression now if no red flags; strong compression after the ABPI.

items.why: Oedema and obesity make pulses unreliable, and ABPI quantifies supply.
items.fix: Arrange ABPI and ask about rest pain and claudication.

items.why: NG152: offer antibiotics only for signs of infection.
items.fix: Explain colonisation and give infection signs.

items.why: CG168 recommends referral for an ulcer not healed within 2 weeks.
items.fix: Refer for duplex and venous treatment.
Agree that compression is the treatment and explain the safe order.

items.fail: No advice on what to do if the bandage causes problems.
items.why: Ischaemia under compression needs immediate action.
items.fix: “If the foot goes cold, pale or very painful, take it off and call us.”

wordPics.fail: Applies tight compression on request without an ABPI, or refuses any bandage without explanation; prescribes antibiotics for a colonised ulcer; does not check the pulses; no safety-net.
wordPics.pass: Recognises a venous ulcer, explains that ABPI is needed before strong compression, refers to the leg-ulcer nurses, and safety-nets for infection and ischaemia.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: explains the risk in plain words; offers safe mild compression now in line with NWCSP; refers to vascular per CG168; applies NG152 stewardship; keeps malignancy in mind; sets realistic healing expectations; checks understanding with teach-back.

avoid.instead: “Tight bandaging is the right treatment once we’ve checked your circulation with an ankle test.”
avoid.why: Strong compression on an arterial leg can cause necrosis.

avoid.dont: “Let’s do a swab and start antibiotics.”
avoid.instead: “Antibiotics only help if it becomes infected. Here’s what to look for.”
avoid.why: NG152: most ulcers are colonised, not infected.

avoid.dont: “It’ll be healed in a couple of weeks.”
avoid.instead: “Most heal with the right treatment, but it usually takes weeks to months.”
avoid.why: False expectations damage trust and adherence.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: [1] National Wound Care Strategy Programme (NWCSP) Leg ulcer recommendations (2020, updated 2023) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · [2] NICE CG168 Varicose veins: diagnosis and management (2013) · [3] NICE NG152 Leg ulcer infection: antimicrobial prescribing (2020) · [5] NICE CG147 Peripheral arterial disease (2012, updated 2020)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A classic venous leg ulcer in the gaiter area. Compression heals it, but strong compression must wait for an ABPI to exclude arterial disease. Mild compression can start now if there are no red flags. Refer to the vascular service, treat infection only if present, and keep malignancy in mind if it does not heal.

points.t: Venous: medial gaiter area, shallow, sloping edges, exudate, haemosiderin staining, varicose eczema, oedema, often less painful. Arterial: distal or over pressure points, punched out, deep, painful especially at night or on elevation and eased by hanging the leg down, cold pale foot, weak or absent pulses. Neuropathic: pressure points in people with diabetes, often painless.

NWCSP [1]: if there are no red flags and no signs of arterial disease, start mild graduated compression (20 mmHg or less at the ankle) straight away, and complete a full assessment including ABPI, normally within 14 days. Strong, full compression, which is what “bandaged tight” means, is applied only after the ABPI. If the ABPI is below 0.8 or above 1.3, get specialist advice before compression.

Strong compression on a leg with poor arterial supply can cause ischaemia, necrosis and limb loss. Pulses alone are unreliable, especially with oedema and obesity. In diabetes, ABPI can be falsely normal or raised because the arteries are stiff [5].

CG168 [2]: refer people with a venous leg ulcer (a break in the skin below the knee that has not healed within 2 weeks) or a healed venous leg ulcer to a vascular service for duplex assessment and treatment of the underlying veins.

NG152 [3]: most leg ulcers are colonised and few are infected. Offer an antibiotic only if there are symptoms or signs of infection, such as redness or swelling spreading beyond the ulcer, local warmth, increased pain or fever. Do not swab routinely.

Rolled or everted edges, overgrown tissue, bleeding, an unusual site, or failure to heal despite good treatment should prompt reassessment and biopsy. NICE NG12 [4]: consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for a skin lesion that raises the suspicion of squamous cell carcinoma.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Let her explain and took the neighbour’s bandage request seriously.
Mobility, weight, how she manages dressings and the embarrassment of exudate.
Picked up “bandaged tight” as the key safety issue, and the worry that it will never heal.
Idea (tight bandage will cure it), concern (never healing, embarrassment), expectation (bandage today).
Inspected both legs and the wound on video, used the recorded pulses and sensation; planned ABPI; considered bloods including HbA1c.
Venous versus arterial, mixed, neuropathic and malignant ulcers.
Screened for arterial rest pain, claudication, infection and atypical features.
Named a venous leg ulcer and explained why pulses alone cannot clear her for strong compression.
Mild compression now if no red flags; strong compression after ABPI; leg-ulcer nursing and vascular referral.
Antibiotics only if infected; emollient for varicose eczema; weight and mobility support offered.
Remove bandage and call for a cold, pale or painful foot; infection signs; biopsy if not healing; review after ABPI.

social.t: Reduced mobility and weight make elevation, calf exercise and dressing changes harder. Ask what help she has at home and whether she can reach the leg-ulcer clinic or needs district nurses.
Leaking exudate is embarrassing and isolating. Good dressings and compression reduce it.

legal.t: Explain the benefits and risks of compression, including what to do if the foot becomes cold or painful, and record her consent.

professional.t: Practice nurses, district nurses, the tissue viability team and the vascular service share care. A clear referral and a documented ABPI keep the plan safe.
Apply NICE NG152: treat infection, not colonisation, and avoid routine swabs.

community.t: Community leg-ulcer clinics or leg clubs, where available, offer treatment and social contact. Legs Matter provides patient information.

redFlags: Rest pain at night or on elevation, cold or pale foot: arterial disease
Spreading redness, warmth, increasing pain or fever: infection
Rolled or everted edges, bleeding, overgrowth or failure to heal: possible SCC
Diabetes: neuropathic ulcer and unreliable ABPI
ice: Idea: a tight bandage will cure it, as it did for her neighbour
Concern: that it will never heal

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This is a venous leg ulcer. The veins in your leg aren’t pushing blood back up efficiently, so the pressure in the skin near the ankle is high and it breaks down.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Imagine the veins as a pipe with one-way valves. When the valves are leaky, fluid pools at the ankle like water at the bottom of a hose. The bandage squeezes it back up. But we must check the supply pipe, the arteries, is open before we squeeze hard.”

management.reflectIce: “You’re right that a firm bandage is the treatment. We’re doing it safely: a light one now, and the full one once the test shows your circulation can take it.”
management.psychosocial: Arrange nursing care she can reach, support elevation and mobility, and offer weight support if she wants it.
sharedPlan: Mild compression now (no red flags), ABPI within 14 days (NWCSP)
Strong compression if ABPI 0.8–1.3; specialist advice otherwise
Dressings, emollient for varicose eczema, elevation
Antibiotics only if infected (NG152); consider HbA1c
safetyNet: Remove bandage and call same day for a cold, pale, blue or very painful foot
Call for spreading redness, heat or fever
Biopsy if not healing or atypical; review after ABPI

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station hinges on one safety step. Candidates fail by bandaging on request or by refusing without explaining. The marks go to a safe compression plan, clear reasons, and stewardship.

items.fail: Applying strong compression without an ABPI.
items.why: Compression on a leg with arterial disease can cause necrosis.
items.fix: Mild compression now if no red flags; strong compression after the ABPI.

items.why: Oedema and obesity make pulses unreliable, and ABPI quantifies supply.
items.fix: Arrange ABPI and ask about rest pain and claudication.

items.why: NG152: offer antibiotics only for signs of infection.
items.fix: Explain colonisation and give infection signs.

items.why: CG168 recommends referral for an ulcer not healed within 2 weeks.
items.fix: Refer for duplex and venous treatment.
Agree that compression is the treatment and explain the safe order.

items.fail: No advice on what to do if the bandage causes problems.
items.why: Ischaemia under compression needs immediate action.
items.fix: “If the foot goes cold, pale or very painful, take it off and call us.”
